finding: The phase III paragraph omits publicly posted final results for NCT05754333. The endpoint was surgeon-rated ureter conspicuity, so this is stronger visualization evidence but still does not establish fewer ureteral injuries.
evidence: EU Clinical Trials Register EudraCT 2025-000122-33, https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2025-000122-33/results (opened): explicitly links NCT05754333, 107 enrolled; in the primary 72-adult normal/mild renal-function cohort after 3 mg IV, mean 30-minute white-light and NIR scores were 2.7 and 4.3, paired difference 1.5 points (95% CI 1.2–1.9; p<0.001). Results version 2 was posted November 15, 2025.

edit.old: **Phase III:** ClinicalTrials.gov lists two completed phase III ureter-visualization studies, NCT05754333 (n=107, completed January 2025) and NCT05999747 (n=95, including participants with kidney disease, completed October 2025). Peer-reviewed results have not yet appeared.<sup>[[6]](#ref6)</sup>
edit.new: **Phase III:** NCT05754333 enrolled 107 participants; sponsor-posted final results report a 1.5-point higher mean ureter-conspicuity score with NIR than white light at 30 minutes (95% CI 1.2–1.9) among 72 adults with normal or mildly impaired renal function given 3 mg IV. This surrogate endpoint does not establish injury prevention. NCT05999747 enrolled 95 participants; a peer-reviewed phase III report was not identified.<sup>[[6]](#ref6)[[7]](#ref7)</sup>

finding: The categorical contrast with methylene blue is false: IV methylene blue has produced NIR ureter images in humans, albeit with a different imaging system and off-label use.
evidence: PMID 23466242, DOI 10.1016/j.juro.2013.02.3187, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23466242/ (opened): a 12-patient prospective feasibility study used IV methylene blue with Mini-FLARE near-infrared imaging and visualized both ureters within 10 minutes.

edit.old: methylene blue is visible rather than NIR
edit.new: methylene blue has also been used for NIR ureter imaging on a compatible system in a small human study<sup>[[8]](#ref8)</sup>

finding: The early statement that 1 mg and 3 mg gave fluorescence for the duration of cases makes intermittent observation sound continuous and omits the 1 mg failure. The study's primary endpoint required fluorescence at 30 minutes and at the end of surgery.
evidence: PMID 37474823, DOI 10.1007/s00464-023-10193-9, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00464-023-10193-9 (opened full text): the primary endpoint was positive visualization at both time points; success was 5/6 at 1 mg and 3/3 at 3 mg, with observations at specified intervals.

edit.old: In the phase II study, 1 mg and 3 mg IV gave ureteral fluorescence for the duration of laparoscopic colorectal cases.
edit.new: In the 12-patient phase II colorectal study, 1 mg and 3 mg IV met the two-time-point visualization endpoint in 5/6 and 3/3 participants, respectively.

finding: The current description of indigo carmine's supply as unreliable conflicts with the linked indigo-carmine page, which says the shortage ended and BLUDIGO has a current US label. Historical shortage should not drive a present-day alternative choice.
evidence: DailyMed BLUDIGO current label, https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=73f246c4-b127-452e-856f-134b56cb8870 (opened): labeled IV visualization aid for adult cystoscopic ureteral assessment; the linked docs/01-foundations/pharmacology/intraoperative-adjuncts/visualization-agents/indigo-carmine.mdx states the 2014 shortage is over and advises checking local supply.

edit.old: indigo carmine is a visible dye whose supply has been unreliable
edit.new: indigo carmine is a visible dye with a current US BLUDIGO label for cystoscopic ureteral assessment; local supply still requires confirmation

finding: The text suggests broad compatibility with existing NIR platforms while saying compatibility is unestablished. The human feasibility trial actually identified one tested platform; performance on other platforms was not shown.
evidence: PMID 37474823, DOI 10.1007/s00464-023-10193-9, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00464-023-10193-9 (opened full text, Methods): index ureters were imaged with the Stryker 1688 AIM 4K platform; no Firefly, SPY, or Rubina comparison was reported.

edit.old: Pudexacianinium is designed to combine IV convenience with NIR imaging on existing NIR camera platforms, though camera compatibility is not established (below).
edit.new: Pudexacianinium combined IV administration with NIR imaging on the Stryker 1688 AIM platform in phase II; compatibility with other NIR systems requires device-specific validation.

finding: The proposed suitability for reoperative or irradiated fields reads as a demonstrated clinical use, although the cited phase II series was limited to laparoscopic colorectal surgery and excluded retroperitoneal fibrosis. Preserve the rationale while marking those settings untested.
evidence: PMID 37474823, DOI 10.1007/s00464-023-10193-9, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00464-023-10193-9 (opened full text, Methods): 12 adults underwent laparoscopic colorectal procedures; known retroperitoneal fibrosis was an exclusion criterion. EU trial results https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2025-000122-33/results (opened) report mixed abdominopelvic surgery but no reoperative/irradiated-field subgroup result.

edit.old: which suits robotic pelvic surgery such as sacrocolpopexy, hysterectomy, deep endometriosis and colorectal resection, and reoperative or irradiated fields
edit.new: a potentially useful workflow in pelvic surgery; performance specifically in sacrocolpopexy, deep endometriosis, and reoperative or irradiated fields remains unestablished

finding: The 64% severe-impairment urinary recovery figure is real but heavily influenced by one anomalous participant with suspected extravascular injection. The paper reports about 80% recovery after excluding that participant; readers need that sensitivity analysis before inferring reduced urinary signal.
evidence: PMID 42032338, DOI 10.1007/s00228-026-04063-1, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00228-026-04063-1 (opened full text, Results/Discussion): six severe-impairment participants were enrolled, one excluded from PK analysis for suspected extravascular administration; 48-hour mean recovery was 64% in the severe group and about 80% after the anomalous participant was excluded.

edit.old: In the phase I study, 64% of the dose was recovered unchanged in urine over 48 hours in severe renal impairment versus at least 90% in the other groups; no CKD dose rule has been established.
edit.new: In six participants with severe renal impairment, mean 48-hour urinary recovery was 64%, rising to about 80% after exclusion of one participant with anomalous concentrations and suspected extravascular administration; other groups had at least 90% recovery. No clinical CKD dose rule has been established.
